referencing.rule: All references to cases and legislation should be in-text. Footnotes are not required.

referencing.title: Case law

criteria.label: High Distinction
criteria.text: Provides a well-structured response, with no organisational or clarity issues. Demonstrates excellent identification of relevant legal issues and sub-issues, with at most a single minor oversight that does not significantly impact the overall analysis. States applicable law accurately, completely and precisely with citations in accordance with instructions. Does not include irrelevant issues or law, demonstrating excellent discernment and focus. Applies the law to facts thoroughly and logically, addressing all relevant aspects.  Provides a clear, well-reasoned conclusion that follows logically from the analysis.

criteria.label: Distinction
criteria.text: Provides a good structured response, with only minor organisational or clarity issues. Demonstrates strong identification of relevant legal issues and sub-issues, with a few minor oversights that do not significantly impact the overall analysis. Mostly states applicable law accurately and in accordance with instructions with only minor omissions or errors in completeness or precision. May include an irrelevant issue or law but it does not undermine the response. Applies law to facts well, with only minor gaps in reasoning or analysis. Provides a sound conclusion that may include slight inconsistencies or lack of clarity.

criteria.label: Credit
criteria.text: Provides adequate structure with some organisational or clarity issues present. Demonstrates adequate identification of relevant legal issues and sub-issues, with some notable omissions or inaccuracies. States applicable law generally correctly but lacks some detail or precision. May include some irrelevant issues or laws, but not to the extent that significantly undermines the response. Satisfactorily applies applicable law to facts, but may contain moderate gaps in reasoning or analysis. Provides a reasonable conclusion but lacks some depth.

criteria.label: Pass
criteria.text: Some attempt at structure but with organisational or clarity issues that impact the response to a significant extent. Identifies some relevant issues and/or sub-issues but misses key aspects of the problem. States some applicable law but with significant omissions or inaccuracies. Includes irrelevant issues or law to an extent that demonstrates a limited ability to discern importance. Attempts to apply law to facts but with significant logical gaps or misunderstandings. Provides a basic conclusion that doesn't fully align with the analysis.

criteria.label: Fail
criteria.text: Lacks clear structure or is difficult to follow due to very poor organisation or writing. Fails to identify most of the relevant legal issues, demonstrating a lack of understanding of the core legal problems presented. Fails to state most of the applicable law or states them with significant inaccuracy. Includes a significant amount of irrelevant issues or law, as if reciting notes indiscriminately, significantly undermining the response. Fails to apply law to facts coherently or misapplies law significantly. Fails to provide a conclusion or provides one that doesn't follow from the analysis.

tips.title: Make your own notes
tips.text: The learning comes from selecting and organising the material yourself; exchanged or bought notes may not make sense under pressure.
tips.speaker: Speaker0

tips.title: Compress in stages
tips.text: Unify lecture, tutorial and reading notes into a long set, then a smaller set, then your final concise exam prompts. The process builds the structure of the subject in memory.
tips.speaker: Speaker1

tips.title: Keep notes legible
tips.text: Use clear headings, spacing and a consistent colour or symbol system. Tiny type and packed margins make retrieval slower. Notes should trigger knowledge, not teach the unit during the exam.
tips.speaker: Speakers0,2,3

tips.title: Follow the syllabus
tips.text: Check coverage week by week in the unit’s order. Use lectures as the starting point and attend to authorities highlighted by the lecturer.
tips.speaker: Speakers3,4

tips.title: Build authority tables
tips.text: A useful three-column structure is issue or element; authority and legal rule; important facts and the principle. Organise it in a way you can actually use.
tips.speaker: Speaker5

tips.title: Use diagrams and Cornell prompts
tips.text: Diagram parties or important facts. A Cornell-style layout can pair a short cue with facts or keywords and end with a single-sentence explanation of the authority.
tips.speaker: Speaker6

tips.title: Practise using your notes
tips.text: Compile notes and use them in practice questions before the exam. Knowing the material well matters more than carrying a dense set of pages.
tips.speaker: Speakers2,5

tips.title: Budget time by marks
tips.text: Know the number, types and weights of questions beforehand; allocate time proportionally and stick to the budget so every required question receives an answer.
tips.speaker: Speakers0,1,3,4,6

tips.title: Read the actual question
tips.text: Answer the precise question and apply the particular facts. A general account of a topic, however accurate, may not answer what was asked.
tips.speaker: Speakers1,2

tips.title: Plan when writing is permitted
tips.text: Make a brief thumbnail plan of issues, elements, crucial facts and provisional conclusions before a handwritten answer. For PIL, do this only after the no-writing reading period ends.
tips.speaker: Speakers0,3,4

tips.title: Make the structure visible
tips.text: Use headings and subheadings. Introduce the issue, give the relevant rule, apply it and reach a supported conclusion; avoid irrelevant fact summaries and indiscriminate note dumping.
tips.speaker: Speakers0,1,6

tips.title: Keep a party map
tips.text: For a crowded hypothetical, a small diagram of people, corporations or properties can prevent name confusion and repeated rereading. Draw it only when writing is allowed.
tips.speaker: Speaker4

tips.title: Notice the hidden fact
tips.text: Your plan should capture the subtle fact or difficult element the examiner planted, as well as the obvious issues. Use the plan to adjust depth as time passes.
tips.speaker: Speaker4

tips.title: Use bullets only as a fallback
tips.text: If time is running out, brief points, authorities and conclusions can show knowledge that would otherwise be lost. This is a last resort, not a replacement for a reasoned response.
tips.speaker: Speakers4,5

tips.title: Practise handwriting under time
tips.text: Timed handwritten answers reveal your practical writing speed. Practise concise, relevant analysis and completing the whole paper.
tips.speaker: Speaker6

tips.text: Know the number, types and weights of questions beforehand; allocate time proportionally and stick to the budget so every required question receives an answer.
tips.speaker: Speakers0,1,3,4,6

tips.title: Read the actual question
tips.text: Answer the precise question and apply the particular facts. A general account of a topic, however accurate, may not answer what was asked.
tips.speaker: Speakers1,2

tips.title: Plan when writing is permitted
tips.text: Make a brief thumbnail plan of issues, elements, crucial facts and provisional conclusions before a handwritten answer. For PIL, do this only after the no-writing reading period ends.
tips.speaker: Speakers0,3,4

tips.title: Make the structure visible
tips.text: Use headings and subheadings. Introduce the issue, give the relevant rule, apply it and reach a supported conclusion; avoid irrelevant fact summaries and indiscriminate note dumping.
tips.speaker: Speakers0,1,6

tips.title: Keep a party map
tips.text: For a crowded hypothetical, a small diagram of people, corporations or properties can prevent name confusion and repeated rereading. Draw it only when writing is allowed.
tips.speaker: Speaker4

tips.title: Notice the hidden fact
tips.text: Your plan should capture the subtle fact or difficult element the examiner planted, as well as the obvious issues. Use the plan to adjust depth as time passes.
tips.speaker: Speaker4

tips.title: Use bullets only as a fallback
tips.text: If time is running out, brief points, authorities and conclusions can show knowledge that would otherwise be lost. This is a last resort, not a replacement for a reasoned response.
tips.speaker: Speakers4,5

tips.title: Practise handwriting under time
tips.text: Timed handwritten answers reveal your practical writing speed. Practise concise, relevant analysis and completing the whole paper.
tips.speaker: Speaker6

timetableInstructions.text: The Notes column gives each unit’s primary delivery/attendance mode. Students are expected to sit in that mode; check the unit iLearn site for more specific details.

specialConsideration.title: Serious unavoidable difficulty
specialConsideration.text: The timetable states that serious and unavoidable difficulties at exam time may make a student eligible to apply for Special Consideration. Check the current application process, documents and timeframes.

specialConsideration.title: Unwell before starting
specialConsideration.text: The timetable says that, in general, attempting an exam makes a student ineligible for Special Consideration for that exam; if unwell before it starts, do not attempt it and consult Special Consideration guidance.

specialConsideration.title: Illness during the exam
specialConsideration.text: If unable to continue, stop immediately and tell the supervisor/invigilator. After leaving, check eligibility and apply. Completing without reporting the issue at the time will generally prevent a later illness-based application from being accepted.
